content.text:
# Hartwell Supply Co.: what you're looking at

Hartwell is a family-held HVAC/R distributor: about 150 people, twelve branches (Columbus, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Dayton, Toledo, Akron, Indianapolis, Fort Wayne, Louisville, Lexington, Troy MI and Pittsburgh), selling equipment, parts, refrigerant and supplies to heating and cooling contractors. The records run from 2016 to 2025.

**Its systems, each a separate database copied into the warehouse:**
- **ERP** (`erp_*`): customers and their account managers, the sales reps, products and vendors, sales orders and their lines (how each order arrived and who keyed it), purchase orders, transfers between branches, and returns.
- **Warehouse management** (`wms_*`): every stock movement (opening balances, receipts, sales, transfers, returns) and goods receipts. Stock on hand isn't stored anywhere: it's the running total of the movements.
- **Accounting** (`finance_*`): invoices and their lines, credit memos, customer payments, vendor bills and their lines, and vendor payments.
- **CRM** (`crm_*`): calls and emails to customer service, as logged by whoever took them; and the reps' quotes, with each quote's lines, its outcome (won, lost or expired), a loss reason when the rep entered one, and the order a won quote became.
- **External** (`external_*`): real monthly heating and cooling degree days and residential building permits for each branch's county.

**Days.** `day` is an operating day, about 21 a month; `dim_date` gives the calendar date.

**What isn't here:** profitability by customer, rep or branch; why a return happened; whether an order was keyed correctly; whether a vendor bill was right. Like any real business, those have to be worked out from the records, and some of them can't be.

input.sql:
WITH base AS (SELECT i.customer_id, d.year, i.amount, greatest(p.day-i.due_day,0) late FROM finance_invoices i JOIN finance_customer_payments p USING(invoice_id) JOIN dim_date d ON d.day=i.day JOIN erp_customers c ON c.customer_id=i.customer_id WHERE c.terms_days>0),
tr AS (SELECT customer_id, sum(amount*late)/sum(amount) wl FROM base WHERE year BETWEEN 2016 AND 2019 GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>=10),
s AS (SELECT customer_id, CASE WHEN wl<6 THEN 'A' WHEN wl<20 THEN 'B' ELSE 'C' END seg FROM tr),
t AS (SELECT b.*, s.seg FROM base b JOIN s USING(customer_id) WHERE b.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2024),
ra AS (SELECT sum(amount*late)/sum(amount) a_rate FROM t WHERE seg='A'),
rb AS (SELECT sum(amount*late)/sum(amount) b_rate FROM t WHERE seg='B')
SELECT a_rate, b_rate,
 (sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount*late END) - sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount END)*a_rate)/252/5 c_to_A_bal,
 (sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount*late END) - sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount END)*b_rate)/252/5 c_to_B_bal,
 (sum(CASE WHEN seg='B' THEN amount*late END) - sum(CASE WHEN seg='B' THEN amount END)*a_rate)/252/5 b_to_A_bal,
 (sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount*late END) - sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount END)*a_rate)/252/5*0.08 c_to_A_8pct,
 (sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount*late END) - sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount END)*b_rate)/252/5*0.05 c_to_B_5pct,
 ((sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount*late END) - sum(CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN amount END)*a_rate)+(sum(CASE WHEN seg='B' THEN amount*late END) - sum(CASE WHEN seg='B' THEN amount END)*a_rate))/252/5*0.08 bc_to_A_8pct,
 count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN seg='C' THEN customer_id END) c_cust
FROM t, ra, rb GROUP BY a_rate, b_rate

content.text:
I've saved the revised F7 as `finding.json`. I accepted all seven of the challenger's points and rebutted none. The core finding still holds, but it's now narrower and the headline dollar figure is lower.

**What changed:**
- **Headline now comes from an out-of-sample test.** Customers classed as very slow using 2016–19 data alone (152 accounts) went on to hold 29.0% of the 2020–24 overdue balance on 5.3% of billing (q331). That replaces the in-sample 33%. About a fifth of later overdue dollars (18.5%) came from customers who couldn't have been classed in advance.
- **Weaker persistence claim.** "Lateness is a stable trait of each customer" became "which of the three tiers a customer is in stays stable". Within a tier, year-to-year lateness doesn't persist (correlation about 0, q341), so the overall 0.94 only reflects the gaps between tiers. The tier is what to act on; you can't rank individual customers within it.
- **Credit limits reframed.** Equal limits across tiers don't mean credit policy was tried and failed. The limit field doesn't track customer size or lateness at all (q347), so this data can't test whether credit policy matters.
- **2025 low point explained.** The 2025 dip in the very slow tier's share comes from invoices still unpaid at the end of the data, not from improvement (q327). Sizing stays on 2016–24, when every invoice was paid in full.
- **New sizing query (q357).** It measures what a list drawn up in advance would have been worth in 2020–24. Bringing those 152 accounts down to prompt lateness would have released 786,932 of receivables, worth 62,955 a year at an assumed 8%. That is now `dollars_a_year`, replacing 136,567.
- **Dollars shown as a range.** It runs from 30,760 a year (q357: the advance list moved only to slow lateness, at 5%) to 136,567 a year (q343: in-sample slow and very slow tiers both moved to prompt, at 8%). The released cash is a one-time gain; only the carrying cost recurs each year. All figures depend on the assumed rate and don't account for sales that tighter collections might lose; the records can't measure that cost.

The new confounder and seasonality checks also came back null and are now cited as support: size, tenure, discount, credit memos, invoice-question contacts and invoice month don't differ across tiers, and reps account for little if any of it.

The recommendation is the same targeted credit/AR review of the very slow tier, now with a randomised control group. That matters more because the tiers are unusually regular (no persistence within a tier, no seasonality, identical attributes), which may reflect how the records were produced rather than how customers really pay.
